PullRequest.Title: tree: Support sticky sibling nodes in workbench trees

## Summary

Allow tree consumers to make rows sticky without introducing artificial parent/child relationships.

- Add `stickyScrollNodeCandidateProvider` to select rows that stay sticky over the remainder of their actual parent's content. Selected siblings stack in list order, subject to existing item-count and height limits.
- Cache candidates and source-range suppression outside scrolling; document `refreshStickyScroll()` invalidation and forward refresh/rerender through async trees.
- Keep reveal offsets consistent with constrained sticky stacks, preserve untouched sticky DOM during unrelated splices, and prevent compression from joining unrelated sibling headers into ancestor paths.
- Adopt the API in the Agents Window Sessions list: flatten the synthetic header hierarchy and keep **New**, **Sessions**, and structural group headers stacked with correct accessibility levels.

No linked issue. The branch includes current `main` as of the final validation.

## Validation

All checks below passed on the final branch:

```sh
npm run compile-client
```

```sh
node --experimental-strip-types build/hygiene.ts src/vs/base/browser/ui/tree/abstractTree.ts src/vs/base/browser/ui/tree/asyncDataTree.ts src/vs/base/browser/ui/tree/objectTree.ts src/vs/base/test/browser/ui/tree/asyncDataTree.test.ts src/vs/base/test/browser/ui/tree/objectTree.test.ts src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/browser/views/sessionsList.ts src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/test/browser/sessionsList.test.ts
```

```sh
node test/unit/browser/index.js --browser chromium --run src/vs/base/test/browser/ui/tree/objectTree.test.ts --run src/vs/base/test/browser/ui/tree/asyncDataTree.test.ts --run src/vs/sessions/contrib/sessions/test/browser/sessionsList.test.ts
```

**263 passing.** Coverage includes sibling stacking and containment, equal-height splices, async invalidation, compression, focus preservation, constrained reveal, no-op-provider compatibility, and bounded lookup across 1,000 candidates and suppressed prefixes.

```sh
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
```

The Electron unit-test runner crashed at startup during earlier validation; the complete affected suites passed using Chromium. Live-window and screen-reader validation were not performed.

## Manual Testing

1. Open the Agents Window Sessions list with the experimental navigation shown and enough sessions to scroll.
2. Scroll past Automations and Customizations, then into the session content.
3. Verify **New** remains sticky, **Sessions** sticks below it, and the current structural group header can stick below both within the height limit.
4. Open Find, filter sessions, resize the list, and verify header rendering and keyboard focus remain correct.

Scenarios.Scenario: Scroll and reveal the Agents Window Sessions list with New, Sessions, and structural group headers sticky
Scenarios.CriticalPath: A scroll event synchronously recomputes sticky state and updates sticky-row DOM only when state changes; reveal additionally computes the constrained sticky height before adjusting scroll position.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: The visible tree may contain many sessions, but the new consumer selects exactly two custom candidates and sticky traversal/rendering is capped by stickyScrollMaxItemCount (configured as 7 by default).
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Single synchronous UI-thread computation per scroll/layout event; no queue, parallel work, or asynchronous fan-out is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Candidate classification and source-range eligibility are populated on tree splices and reused on warm scrolls. Candidate lookup is binary within each parent, and the provider is not rerun while scrolling. Explicit refresh invalidates and rebuilds the cache.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the synchronous scroll path, cache reuse, two-candidate cardinality, and seven-row rendering bound from the changed implementation and consumer configuration.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Very deep trees can increase ancestry traversal, but this sessions tree has shallow grouping and only two custom candidates; no evidence establishes a user-visible regression on this path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the changed hot path avoids collection scans during scrolling, bounds sticky work, and introduces no subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network boundary.

Scenarios.Scenario: Refresh the visible Sessions list after session/model/group/active-session changes
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The existing update routine rebuilds local section elements and synchronously calls tree.setChildren; the new sticky resolver classifies inserted rendered rows, updates two cached candidates, and recomputes the current sticky state before the list update completes.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Work scales with the number of rendered sessions/rows on a cold or replacement splice; effective custom-candidate cardinality remains two regardless of session count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Updates are synchronous on the UI thread; active-session updates are scheduled to the next animation frame, while other model events invoke one list update. No new concurrency burst or limiter interaction is present.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: A replacement splice invalidates candidate indices and rebuilds classification for inserted rows. Subsequent scrolling is warm-cache. Empty/no-sticky state still evaluates the candidate predicate for inserted rows, but the pre-existing setChildren path already creates and splices the same full rendered collection.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the full-splice call path and linear classification cost; low evidence that its incremental constant-factor work independently creates perceptible latency.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact maximum session count and update frequency are not measured, but the added predicate pass is linear alongside the pre-existing full-tree rebuild and retains only two candidates.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the diff adds bounded cache maintenance to an already collection-wide synchronous rebuild without adding a higher-order cost, expensive boundary, or retained state proportional to all sessions.

Scenarios.Scenario: Use the new sticky sibling provider in a generic ObjectTree or AsyncDataTree across splices, filtering, collapse/expand, and explicit refresh
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Tree rendered-splice and collapse notifications synchronously maintain candidate indices/sections, then recompute sticky state. Explicit refresh scans the current rendered list by contract; warm scrolls use the cache.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Cache maintenance scales with rendered inserted rows plus selected candidate count; tests exercise 1,000 candidates. Recursive collapse can emit multiple collapse notifications, but the only production consumer added here selects two candidates and does not place a large recursive candidate hierarchy on this path.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: All model notifications and cache updates are serialized synchronously on the UI thread; there is no background work, coalescing, or external concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Positive candidates and source-range suppression are cached, removed or reindexed on rendered splices, rebuilt on explicit refresh, and scoped to the tree controller lifetime. Deleted/hidden rendered nodes are removed through splice events; no unbounded cache retention was established.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in cache lifecycle and synchronous event multiplicity from the model implementation; confidence is insufficient that a realistic changed product scenario reaches high candidate cardinality.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Future consumers could select many candidates or combine them with large recursive collapse operations, but no such changed production call site exists in this PR, so that risk is not a concrete diff-triggered product regression.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding: current changed usage keeps candidate cardinality constant, and reporting hypothetical high-cardinality future API use would not meet PR-causality and realistic-trigger requirements.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all seven changed files and all diff pages. Traced sticky-scroll scroll/reveal, sessions refresh, splice/filter, collapse/expand, cache lifecycle, DOM rendering, and transitive expensive boundaries. No high-confidence actionable performance regression introduced by the changed production paths was found.
